opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. Autonomous driving is a really interesting reference point for those of us in robotics, because in many ways it's the field that's furthest along in taking embodied AI out of the lab and into the real world.

My assessment is that the progress has been real but slower than people predicted ten years ago. Around 2015 or 2016, many people believed fully driverless cars would be everywhere within a few years. That didn't happen. The reason is the long tail. Getting a car to drive well 95% or even 99% of the time is relatively achievable. But the remaining cases, an unusual construction zone, a pedestrian doing something unexpected, strange weather, a police officer waving you through a red light, are where most of the effort goes. And for a safety-critical system, you can't ignore those cases.

What's changed in the last few years is that we now have robotaxi services operating without a safety driver in several cities, carrying real passengers every day. That's a meaningful milestone. It shows the technology can reach a level of reliability where people trust it with their lives. And the approach has been shifting from heavily hand-engineered modular pipelines toward more end-to-end, data-driven learning, which scales better as you collect more driving data.

For robotics more broadly, I see two lessons. First, data and scale matter enormously. Autonomous driving had the advantage of millions of cars generating data, and general-purpose robots don't have that yet. That's one of the biggest bottlenecks we face. Second, deployment takes patience. Even after the core technology works, there's a long process of validation, safety, regulation, and building public trust. So when people ask me when we'll have robots in every home, I often point to autonomous driving and say: the demo comes first, then a long journey to reliable, large-scale deployment. Robotics is maybe several years behind driving on that curve, but I think we can move faster because we can learn from what the driving community went through.

r001.rationale: The response treats driverless robotaxi services in several cities as a meaningful milestone, but it does not identify those operations as Waymo’s.

r002.rationale: It describes a long journey from demos or core technology working to reliable, large-scale deployment, including validation, safety, regulation, and public trust.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think we're much further along than most people outside the field realize, but also further from "done" than the headlines suggest. Those two things are both true at once.

If you look at what's actually on the road today, Waymo is running fully driverless paid rides in several US cities, doing hundreds of thousands of trips a week with nobody behind the wheel. Baidu's Apollo Go is doing something similar in Wuhan and a few other Chinese cities. That's not a demo anymore. That's a service that ordinary people use to get to work. Five years ago, a lot of serious people said that wouldn't happen in our lifetime. So on the question of "can a machine drive a car safely in a real city," I think the answer has basically been settled. Yes, it can.

The hard part now is a different question, which is how do you go from a few geofenced cities to everywhere. And that's where I think people underestimate the difficulty. Each new city is not just "copy and paste." You have different road conventions, different weather, different driver behavior, different regulators. The system has to generalize, and the company has to prove to a lot of stakeholders that it generalizes. That's an engineering problem, a data problem, and a trust problem all at the same time.

What's changed on the technical side, and this is what I find most exciting coming from a robotics and learning background, is the shift toward end-to-end learned systems. For a long time, autonomy was a pipeline: perception module, prediction module, planning module, each hand-engineered and tuned separately. Now you're seeing much more of the stack learned jointly from data, and large models, including vision-language models, starting to give these systems something closer to common sense about rare situations. A construction worker waving you through, a ball rolling into the street, a police officer overriding a traffic light. Those long-tail cases used to each require a special rule. Learned systems handle them more gracefully, though they also introduce new challenges around verification.

So my honest assessment: the core capability is here. The next five years are about scale, cost, and the long tail. I'd expect robotaxis to feel normal in maybe a dozen or two major cities by the end of the decade, with personal vehicles getting increasingly capable but still supervised. The last few percent of reliability is where almost all the remaining work is, and that last few percent is not a small thing.

r001.rationale: The response presents Waymo’s driverless paid rides as an active service, not a demo, and says real-city autonomous driving is now a demonstrated capability.

r002.rationale: The response describes the difficulty of expanding from a few operating cities to broader coverage, but does not identify a substantial gap between conceiving the technology and achieving real-world deployment.

astra-6.text:
I think we’ve made substantial progress, but deployment is a much higher bar than demonstrating that a car can drive itself. The question is whether it can operate safely and reliably across the full range of situations it will encounter.

It helps to distinguish deployment in a constrained area from driving anywhere, in any conditions. If you limit the geography, road types, and weather, you have a more manageable problem. Expanding beyond those boundaries means dealing with unusual situations, unpredictable human behavior, and uncertainty.

So I see deployment as a gradual process. The important measures are safety, how much human support the system needs, and whether it can deliver a useful service at a sustainable cost. There’s reason to be optimistic, but I’d be cautious about putting a single timeline on autonomous driving as a whole.

r001.rationale: The response says autonomous driving has made substantial progress and discusses constrained deployment, but it does not mention Waymo or driverless taxis as evidence.

r002.rationale: It says deployment is a much higher bar than demonstrating that a car can drive itself, and describes the safety and reliability demands of real-world operation.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we’ve made real progress, but deployment is much more than getting a car to drive itself in a demonstration. The key question is whether it can operate safely and reliably within a clearly defined set of conditions, and what it does when it reaches the limits of those conditions.

I’d distinguish between deployment in constrained environments and driving everywhere under all circumstances. The first gives us a practical path forward: define the operating area, validate the system carefully, and expand as the evidence supports it. The second is a much harder problem.

So I’m optimistic, but I would measure progress by consistent performance, the quality of safety validation, and how well the system handles unusual situations—not just by how impressive a single drive looks.

r001.rationale: The response discusses progress toward deployment and constrained operating areas, but never identifies Waymo’s driverless taxi operation as evidence.

r002.rationale: It says deployment involves much more than a demonstration and requires safe, reliable operation, validation, and handling unusual situations, conveying a substantial gap between a demonstration and real-world deployment.
